title: Kronecker sums and Sylvester invertibility
subtitle: G2 lecture 064000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 064000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: For diagonal self-adjoint A and B, the Sylvester equation A X minus X B equals C can be solved entry by entry when every cross-spectral difference is nonzero.
body: Here we treat the entire left-hand side as a single linear operator. Its input is a matrix X, and its output is the matrix A X minus X B. Once we understand the spectrum of that operator, we can state precisely when the Sylvester equation has a unique solution for every right-hand side.
There are two reasons to do this. First, it reveals why the differences of eigenvalues are unavoidable.
slides.takeaway: View the Sylvester equation as a single linear problem in mn variables.

slides.title: A linear operator on a space of matrices
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 064000 · A linear operator on a space of matrices
slides.lead: Let A be an m-by-m matrix and B an n-by-n matrix.
body: The unknown X has m rows and n columns. The space of possible X matrices is a vector space of dimension m times n. Define a map S by the rule: S applied to X equals A X minus X B.

Multiplication distributes over sums, so S is linear. Solving the Sylvester equation means solving S of X equals C. Why bother naming this map? Because we can ask ordinary questions about its kernel, eigenvalues, determinant, and inverse.
slides.takeaway: Linearization moves from matrix entries to the vector space of matrices.
slides.mathtex: \mathcal S_{A,B}:\mathbb C^{m\times n}\to\mathbb C^{m\times n},\quad X\mapsto AX-XB

slides.title: Stacking columns into a vector
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 064000 · Stacking columns into a vector
slides.lead: Column stacking produces an explicit mn-by-mn matrix.
body: For an m-by-n unknown X, column vectorization sends AX to (Iₙ⊗A)vec(X), while XB becomes (Bᵀ⊗Iₘ)vec(X). Their difference is a single linear system in mn scalar coordinates.
The transpose arises because right multiplication combines columns; ignoring it is a common mistake when writing the Kronecker representation.
slides.takeaway: The Kronecker sum is the matrix of the Sylvester operator in vec coordinates.

slides.title: A diagonal example
slides.lead: Take A diagonal with entries one and four, and B diagonal with entries zero and three.
body: Use column-stacking order. The first column of X has spectral differences one minus zero and four minus zero. Those are one and four. The second column has differences one minus three and four minus three. Those are negative two and one.

Therefore the four-by-four matrix of S is diagonal with entries one, four, negative two, one. Its determinant is negative eight, so the map is invertible. For any right-hand side, invert this diagonal matrix by dividing the four coordinates by those entries.
slides.takeaway: Matrix units become eigenvectors when the coefficients are diagonal.

slides.title: Why all eigenvalue differences occur
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 064000 · Why all eigenvalue differences occur
slides.lead: The diagonal calculation proves the claim for diagonal matrices.
body: But the spectrum of S is determined by cross differences even when A and B are not self-adjoint or diagonalizable, provided we work with finite complex matrices. Here is a route to the general statement. Every complex square matrix has an eigenvector.

Starting with that eigenvector and extending to a basis puts the matrix into upper block-triangular form. Repeat on the remaining block. Induction gives an upper-triangular matrix, even when no eigenbasis exists. Apply this procedure separately to A and B.
slides.takeaway: All cross-eigenvalue differences appear in the Sylvester operator spectrum.

slides.title: Invertibility and disjoint spectra
slides.lead: The spectrum of the Sylvester map contains every left-right difference.
body: In a diagonal basis each matrix unit Eᵢⱼ satisfies S(Eᵢⱼ)=(aᵢ−bⱼ)Eᵢⱼ. In the general complex finite-dimensional case, triangularizing A and B produces the same diagonal differences.
Thus the Sylvester map is invertible precisely when the coefficient spectra have no common point. The argument does not require A or B to be invertible.
slides.takeaway: The spectra must be disjoint for the Sylvester map to be invertible.

slides.title: Being invertible is not the same as being well conditioned
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 064000 · Being invertible is not the same as being well conditioned
slides.lead: Disjoint spectra guarantee invertibility, but nonnormal matrices can make the inverse very large.
body: Let A have rows (1,M) and (0,1), while B is the scalar zero operator. Both eigenvalues of A equal one, so the spectral distance from B is always one, whatever the value of M.

But A is nonnormal for nonzero M. Its inverse has rows (1,−M) and (0,1). Applied to the second standard basis vector, the inverse produces (−M,1), with norm √(M²+1). Thus the inverse norm grows without changing the eigenvalue gap.
slides.takeaway: The spectral gap controls conditioning directly for normal coefficients, not for arbitrary nonnormal matrices.

slides.title: The same coordinate-free operator
slides.lead: In the bounded-operator setting, S acts on a space of bounded linear maps between two Banach spaces.
body: It is still linear, and it is bounded because the triangle inequality gives the norm of S applied to X at most the sum of the norms of A and B times the norm of X.

For finite-dimensional coefficients, disjoint spectra give invertibility via triangularization. For bounded operators on complex Banach spaces, the analogous result follows by a contour integral of resolvents. Both arguments concern the same coordinate-free Sylvester map.
slides.takeaway: Unitary diagonalization changes coordinates without changing the map.

slides.title: The mathematical relationship
slides.lead: In the bounded-operator setting, S acts on a space of bounded linear maps between two Banach spaces.
body: It is still linear, and it is bounded because the triangle inequality gives the norm of S applied to X at most the sum of the norms of A and B times the norm of X.
slides.takeaway: Kronecker form and spectral blocks describe the same operator.

slides.title: Invertibility versus numerical stability
slides.lead: The Kronecker matrix shows where the Sylvester spectrum comes from.
body: Triangularization gives the eigenvalues aᵢ−bⱼ of the mn-dimensional Sylvester map. Disjoint spectra are exactly the finite-dimensional invertibility criterion. A tiny nonzero spectral difference produces a large inverse in Hilbert–Schmidt norm for normal coefficients.
The form I⊗A−Bᵀ⊗I is useful for computation; the map X↦AX−XB remains the coordinate-free definition.
slides.takeaway: Solve linear systems on the matrix space, not by separately inverting A and B.
